questions.prompt: A system has m resources of one type shared by three processes A, B and C with peak demands of 3, 4 and 6 respectively. What is the minimum value of m that guarantees deadlock can never occur?
questions.explanation: The worst case gives every process one short of its peak: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 units held with everyone blocked. One more unit lets some process finish and release, so m = 11 suffices.

questions.prompt: A system has 6 identical resources shared by N processes, each of which may request at most 2. For which value of N could deadlock occur?
questions.explanation: Deadlock is impossible while m is at least N(k-1)+1, that is 6 >= N + 1, so N up to 5 is safe. With N = 6 each process can hold one unit and wait for a second, exhausting all six.

questions.prompt: Three processes share 4 instances of a resource, each requesting and releasing one instance at a time. What is the largest maximum demand K per process that still always avoids deadlock?
questions.explanation: Safety requires 4 >= 3(K-1)+1, so 3 >= 3(K-1), giving K = 2. With K = 3 each process could hold one instance and still need two more, with only one instance left over.

questions.prompt: A system contains three programs, each requiring three tape units. What is the minimum number of tape units the system must have so that deadlock can never arise?
questions.explanation: Each program can hold at most two units without completing, so 3 x 2 = 6 units can be tied up. A seventh unit always lets one program reach its requirement and finish, releasing its units.

questions.prompt: In a resource allocation graph where every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle implies:

options.text: Deadlock may or may not have occurred
Deadlock has definitely occurred
The system is in a safe state
Starvation but never deadlock

questions.explanation: With single instances a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. When resource types have several instances a cycle is only necessary, so deadlock becomes possible rather than certain.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an unsafe state under the Banker's algorithm is correct?

options.text: An unsafe state cannot be entered by any request
An unsafe state is always deadlocked
Every state with a blocked process is unsafe
An unsafe state may still avoid deadlock, depending on future requests

questions.explanation: Unsafe means no ordering is guaranteed to let every process finish in the worst case. If processes happen not to claim their full maximum, the system can still complete, the Banker's algorithm is conservative by design.

questions.prompt: Which deadlock prevention policy works by attacking the circular wait condition?

options.text: Numbering resources uniquely and requiring requests in increasing order
Allowing the system to preempt resources from a waiting process
Requiring every process to acquire all resources before it starts
Making all resources shareable

questions.explanation: A global ordering makes a cycle impossible, since a cycle would require some process to request a lower-numbered resource while holding a higher one. Option A attacks hold-and-wait and option C attacks no-preemption.

questions.prompt: An operating system requires a process to release all its resources before requesting another. Which statement is TRUE?

options.text: It prevents starvation but not deadlock
It prevents both deadlock and starvation
It prevents deadlock but can cause starvation
It prevents neither deadlock nor starvation

questions.explanation: Since no process ever holds one resource while waiting for another, hold-and-wait is eliminated and deadlock cannot occur. But a process may repeatedly lose its resources and be forced to restart, so it can starve.

questions.prompt: Consider n processes where process i holds Xi instances of a resource R and may request Yi more, with all instances of R currently in use. Exactly two processes p and q have Yp = Yq = 0. What guarantees that no process other than p and q can complete?

options.text: The total of all Xi exceeds the number of instances of R
Every other process has Yi greater than the sum of Xp and Xq
Every other process has Yi equal to zero
Some other process has Yi less than Xp

questions.explanation: Only p and q can finish immediately, releasing Xp + Xq instances between them. If every remaining process needs strictly more than that, none can proceed even after both release.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock?

options.text: Preemption of allocated resources
Hold and wait
Mutual exclusion
Circular wait

questions.explanation: Deadlock requires NO preemption; resources must not be forcibly taken back. Allowing preemption is in fact one of the standard ways to prevent deadlock.
